content: Dental fluorosis is a condition that arises due to the excessive intake of fluoride. This can occur through various sources such as naturally occurring fluoride in water, water fluoridation, fluoride-containing toothpaste, or other fluoride-rich products. The damage to tooth development typically occurs between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, during which overexposure to fluoride interferes with the normal formation of dental enamel. Teeth are primarily composed of hydroxyapatite and carbonated hydroxyapatite. When fluoride is present during enamel formation, it leads to the creation of fluorapatite. However, excessive fluoride exposure can result in visible changes to the teeth, including yellowing, white spots, and pitting or mottling of the enamel. These changes can make the teeth appear aesthetically unpleasing. It is important to note that dental fluorosis cannot develop once the teeth have erupted into the oral cavity. At this stage, fluorapatite is beneficial as it enhances the teeth's resistance to acid dissolution (demineralization). While permanent teeth are most commonly affected by fluorosis, primary teeth can occasionally exhibit signs of the condition. In mild cases, the enamel may show small white flecks or pits. In more severe cases, brown stains may develop on the teeth. Differential diagnoses for dental fluorosis include Turner's hypoplasia (which is usually more localized), mild forms of amelogenesis imperfecta, and other environmental enamel defects characterized by diffuse or demarcated opacities. The most widely accepted classification system for dental fluorosis is Dean's Fluorosis Index, developed in 1942. This system assigns a fluorosis score based on the most severe form of the condition observed on two or more teeth. Regarding prevalence, national surveys conducted in the United States by the National Institute of Dental Research (1986–1987) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (1999–2002) provide the primary data on dental fluorosis rates. The CDC found a 9% increase in the prevalence of dental fluorosis among American children compared to a similar survey conducted 20 years earlier. Additionally, the data indicate that African Americans experience higher rates of fluorosis compared to Caucasian Americans. The condition is more common in rural areas where drinking water is sourced from shallow wells or hand pumps. It is also more likely to occur in regions where the fluoride content in drinking water exceeds 1 part per million (ppm) and in children with inadequate calcium intake. In areas with water fluoridation at the optimal level of 1 ppm, consuming one liter of water provides 1 milligram of fluoride. It is highly unlikely for an individual to exceed the tolerable upper limit of fluoride intake from optimally fluoridated water alone. However, fluoride consumption can surpass safe levels when individuals consume large amounts of fluoride-containing water in combination with other sources, such as swallowing fluoridated toothpaste, eating foods with high fluoride content, or taking fluoride supplements. The use of fluoride supplements to prevent tooth decay is rare in areas with water fluoridation but was commonly recommended by dentists in the UK until the early 1990s. Preventing dental fluorosis involves reducing fluoride intake to levels below the tolerable upper limit. Treatment for dental fluorosis is primarily cosmetic and can be performed by a dentist. The cost and success of treatment vary depending on the chosen method. Common treatment options include tooth bleaching, microabrasion, and conservative composite restorations or porcelain veneers. Bleaching and microabrasion are typically used for superficial staining, while conservative restorations are employed for more severe aesthetic concerns. As a preventive measure, dentists recommend that children should not receive topical fluoride treatments until the age of three or until an assessment of the child’s total fluoride exposure can be made.
